To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
successful PPCI for AMIs results in a significant release of HFABP and that the quality of coronary blood flow post PPCI as assessed by CTFC does have no influence on this release.

HFABP and Myoglobin are released into the circulation within the first 15 minutes after successful primary PCI in acute myocardial patients and that the quality of the coronary flow post PCI does not influence their release kinetics.
HFABP and MB release kinetics after successful reperfusion are rapid and do not depend on the quality of reflow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of heart fatty acid-binding protein (H-FABP) and its role in the pathogenesis of acute myocardial ischemia.
the study of the kinetics of the release of the biomarkers heart fatty acid-binding protein (HFAB) and myoglobin after percutaneous reperfusion of patients with acute myocardial infarc- tion (AMI).
the study of a group of proteins, which are released in the blood in case of a heart muscle damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HFABP and/or myoglobin are useful markers of reperfusion in the early post-PCI period.

the release of HFABP and MB after successful PPCI in patients with AMI is rapid, with peak levels achieved within 15 minutes and that the quality of reflow does not influence the kinetics of release of these biomarkers in the first two hours after successful PPCI.

HFABP and Myoglobin levels rise within 15 minutes after successful PCI in patients with AMI and that the quality of the coronary flow does not influence the kinetics of the release of these two markers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HFABP is an early biomarker for AMI and its release kinetics is independent from coronary flow.
both HFABP, a novel marker for myocardial injury, and myoglobin, a well-known marker of myocardial injury, are released into the circulation within minutes after successful PPCI in patients with AMI.
HFABP and Myoglobin are released in the circulation after successful revascularization of acute myocardial ischemia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
both HFABP as well as myoglobin can be used as early markers of reperfusion success.
HFABP and MB are released into the circulation in a very early time after successful reperfusion of AMI and the kinetics of release is not dependent on the quality of reflow.
HFABP is a reliable marker to assess the reperfusion status of the myocardium after PPCI.
